newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr set to challenge 78 cts barrier.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr set to challenge 78 cts barrier.

text.p: The Australian dollar kept a firm tone through a quiet Monday as the market consolidated last week's gains and dealers looked forward to more.
Volumes were light and mostly two-way, with bids out of Singapore the only flows of note which helped it edge to a higher close after a steady morning.

The lack of a pullback in the dollar's two week old, two cent wide rally was seen as a bullish omen and dealers looked for a tilt at the 78 cent chart barrier. A break here would be a big step toward reviving last year's uptrend, while rejection could have the currency re-testing the recent US$0.7550 low.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the dollar was poised at US$0.7770/75 against an early US$0.7765/70, having waltzed up from US$0.7740/45 late Friday and US$0.7639/44 a week ago.

It reached as high as US$0.7793 offshore, almost fulfilling an important technical target as 78 cents marks a 38 percent retracement of the fall from December's US$0.8212 top to the US$0.7550 low of February 12.

Clearing this level would open the way to US$0.7850 at least and possibly US$0.7920. Support was nowe pencilled in at US$0.7720 and chart watchers reckoned the upward momentum would last as long as US$0.7680 stayed intact.

The dollar enjoyed a more emphatic uptrend on most crosses courtesy of the paltry interest rates offered in Japan and much of Europe. Profit-taking did pull it back to 1.1377/89 Swiss francs from 1.1391/06 late Friday, but that was not far from a near-five year high of 1.1476 reached offshore.
It was firmer on the yen at 95.26/36 from 95.16/26 and that despite a lapse in US$/yen to 122.55/60 from 123.20/30 in New York, suggesting it was finding demand of its own.
In trade weighted terms the currency was up at 59.5 from 59.3 late Friday, which analysts noted was within spitting distance of the peak of 60.6 reached on December 2.
There were no domestic data due today but wages and investment figures later in the week would provide vital clues on the outlook for monetary policy and growth.

The Department of Industrial Relations December quarter report on wage trends in enterprise bargaining is due Wednesday. Wage rises in the September quarter stood at 4.8 percent across the economy and at 5.3 percent for private sector pay deals alone.
The Reserve Bank has often stated that wage growth of more than 4.5-5.0 percent was incompatible with maintaining underlying inflation in its 2-3 percent target band.
Due on Thursday are final average weekly earnings figures for the November quarter which were originally reported to have risen by a higher than expected 1.2 percent.
Analysts noted the data from the previous two quarters were revised up in their final release.
The data will also include a breakdown between public and private sector wages, which will be important since analysts felt the publis sector may have biased up the overall AWOTE.
If the data does show private sector wages contained it might just leave enough room for the RBA to squeeze in another rate cut should its upbeat view of economy be disappointed.
Private new capital expenditure for the December quarter is due the same day and is expected to show business investment made another healthy contribution to GDP growth.
Forecasts are for a 2.1 percent rise following a 0.9 percent gain in Q3 and a huge 13 percent jump in Q2.

These figures will also include the fifth estimate for investment spending in 1996/97 -- the fourth projected growth of more than 19 percent for the year -- and the first estimate for the 1997/98 financial year.
